en: ‘The youngest of the six lions—
Babadyykan will find his horse,’ they said.
This fame of yours, O hero,
Was known how many years before!
Knowing it, my foal,
Here in this Ak-Talaa,
I waited six years for you.
Of the ruddy wheat,
Take it all, giving not a hair's worth.
Your elder Babadyykan
Speaks a considered word;
Take it into your ears.
On the side of Old Turpan,
Of the accursed Barbar,
At its edge toward sunset,
Along the River Lob,
A waterless desert beyond eyesight,
Lying along its lower reaches,
Without a croaking raven,
At the end of that stretching desert—
Encountered from the unseen,
Karacha, khan of the Noygut,
Had no sons, but many daughters.
By God's loving decree,
It was found for that very man.
Able to chase and stop wild asses,
A pale mare came from the unseen.
His affairs went smoothly as spread ashes.
Among Karacha's countless horses,
Within those countless horses,
She gave birth close to dawn.
Its birth membrane not yet gone,
At birth the foal did not lie down.
Over its mother,
As Karacha watched,
It leaped a full thousand times.
Horse judges and clear-sighted men,
All the knowledgeable examined it.
“This dun one has no master;
If a master appears, he has no sense.
Heed the words we speak;
Find its rightful master.
If you do not find its master,
This dun yearling standing here—
May it not learn of your stinginess,
And tomorrow, on Judgment Day,
Turn you into a black donkey.
This noble creature, the dun yearling,
Has much of the peerless steed in it.
Its mane and tail are embers.
Among round-hoofed horses,
Among hair-tailed steeds,
There is none so formidable.
If ridden on a six-month journey,
It shows the promise of never tiring.
Until sixty years of maturity,
It shows the promise of never aging.
At ‘Go!’ it lets no one catch it;
It shows the nature of a whirlwind.
Its chest is broad, its shoulders narrow;
It shows signs of great prowess.
We looked from every direction;
Its peerless quality appeared.
When we examined it from every side,
It was a hardy, noble warhorse,
One to be found by a fortunate man,
By one whose destined time has come.
The brave man who rides this
Will bring your joy to fulfillment.
If you care for it well,
In the end, one day, Karacha,
It will fill your belly.
Its hair-tail tied tightly up,
This dun yearling standing here
Is a beast to ride into slaughter.
With a covering of protective armor,
It is a beast to ride on campaign.
Unflustered by the sound of shouting,
In the darkness of the moon,
It never places one step wrong.
At the sound of tumult, it stands apart;
Its peerless quality appears.
If the dun yearling lives,
It will become a divinely favored steed.
If it lives, the one
Who asks for it will be a stranger.
Hoe-hoofed, broad-rumped,
The swift steed of the open land,
It is a beast to ride into battle.
Saying, ‘I will not give it,’ raising a quarrel,
Do not throw matters into disorder.
Continually saying, ‘I will not give it freely,’
This dun yearling is a champion;
Do not cut short its long life.
Put a halter on its head.
To a man who knows its fortune,
Open its fortune and sell it.
It is a horse of another kind,
With no master to ride it on campaign.
Trailing its hair-tail,
It is a horse made to go forth.
Into slaughter running red with blood,
It is a horse made to be ridden.
When the earth splits and cannot be seen,
It is a horse to ride into dust.
In a great battle that bends the earth,
It is a horse to ride into blood.
With its covering hanging bulky,
It is a beast to ride into fire.
Where champions stand and fight,
Where heads are cut and blood is shed,
It is a beast to ride to the frontier.
For red spears and swords,
It is a beast to saddle and ride,
Into warfare month after year,
It is a beast to test and ride.
This noble creature, the dun yearling,
The foal of a young mare,
The Duldul among the horse herds,
The precious one among hair-tailed beasts,
The peerless steed among many horses.
Its hooves are most wondrous,
Like platters on which meat is served.
Its rump stands distinct and broad,
Like an open plain spread at ease.
If you look at its white teeth,
Shaped, struck and tempered,
They are like the blacksmiths' steel.
The space between its hind legs is broad,
Like a ravine grown with meadowsweet.
A peerless steed, it surges with spirit.
Into a dungeon forty rope-lengths deep,
Even if you cast it now,
It will meet its fortunate warrior.”
Then to Karacha,
Many judges spoke these words:
“Do not leave it mixed with the herd.
Without finding its master,
Do not slaughter it for nothing.
It will meet a fortunate warrior;
Do not bind its fortune shut.
Put a halter on its head.
To a blue-maned hero who knows its worth,
Present it with your own hands.
Heed the words we speak;
Find its rightful master.
When it reaches full maturity,
Beware, and take thought:
Your horse will vanish then!
It will attain its desire,
Renounce your horse herds,
And go to seek its master.
If you heed my words, Karacha,
On the dun yearling's head,
Put a halter.
Go and seek its master;
Lay the gift before him.
Consider these words of mine.
It is no ordinary mane and tail.
Place a lead-rope on its neck.
Wear horses out scouting roads,
Loose hounds and fly hunting birds,
Find its destined master.
For your gift, abundant property
Take without hesitation.
Listen well to my words.
If you fittingly offer the dun yearling,
It will bring you blessing.
It will fulfill your thoughts.
If the dun yearling lives,
All your chests
It will fill with yellow gold.
It will fulfill your heart's desire.
If the dun yearling lives,
All your coffers
It will fill with abundant gold.
A true peerless steed, the dun yearling
Has the speed of a whirlwind.
It will not stop for any man;
Such is its formidable nature.
Its desire, the dun yearling
Shows the promise of attaining.
Its master, in the end,
It shows the promise of finding and reaching.
This wondrous dun yearling's
Master was born along with it.
If the dun yearling finds its master,
It will bring tumult to the world.
This dun yearling, may it be slaughtered—
Belongs to a back one can lean upon,
To one born above other mortals,
To a lion who will be a support.
Heed the words we speak;
Without grieving over the steed,
Find its rightful master.
You have happened to rear it;
The dun yearling is not your property.
This renowned, wondrous steed
Is no horse for an ordinary mortal to ride.
It has a giant to ride it into battle.
The wretched dun yearling
Has a master it awaits.”
Saying this to Khan Karacha,
The judge returned to his village.
When the year's twelve months were full,
Upon Karacha's people
A famine fell.
Karacha's numerous Noygut,
Lamenting that they could find no grain,
Scattered their four kinds of livestock.
Their strength exhausted, their vigor gone,
The hapless Noygut then
Fled in every direction.
Their people were left weeping:
Locusts had overrun and ravaged their land.
All the people gathered;
When such a calamity came,
All their livestock perished.
Their great people could find no grain
And were sorely distressed, I heard.
What one asks, the Almighty
Will grant, I heard.
The dun colt approaching its fifth year
Has now reached five, they say.
For Karacha, khan of the Noygut,
The time to part with it has come, they say.
Listen to my words:
Give all your wheat
And take the dun colt.
If you gain possession of the dun,
Your hopes will flourish and unfold,
And all misfortune will be cut away.
Khizir will visit and bring you fortune;
The true God will grant you a horse.
Ride it for six months: it will not weaken.
Until it reaches sixty years of maturity,
It will not grow old with worn-out teeth.
Ride it scouting: it will not tire.
Ride it to the rear camp: it will not sicken.
Ride it into gunfire: it will not weaken.
That is the peerless steed.
God Most High, the Almighty,
For the truly fierce-maned Khan Manas
To find, choose, and ride—
That is the horse He has ordained.
A horse descended from the unseen,
Truly surging into the holy war,
It was brought forth for your good fortune.
Such is that wondrous steed:
From the east to the west,
It has strength to run untiringly.
That is the horse to find and ride.
When it treads upon black stone,
The stone crumbles like millet.
Simply give it its head,
And it flies like a cloud with a thunderous rush.
